hints: Think about the difference between counting the actual atoms in a molecule and simplifying that count to the smallest possible whole numbers.
walkthrough:
Separate molecular from empirical**
Think of molecular formula as the true count, for example $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}$ for cyclopentane. Empirical formula simplifies this to the lowest ratio that still shows the relative numbers of each element.

State the definition precisely**
For cycloalkanes the molecular formula $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n}$ simplifies to $\text{CH}_2$, which is why they share the same empirical formula as alkenes. The key words are simplest or lowest whole number ratio of atoms.
Final answer: The simplest whole number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.

hints: Keep the total formula fixed at $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}$ but change the ring size, a 5-membered ring can become a 4-membered or 3-membered ring if you add alkyl side chains to make up the carbons.
Try one isomer based on a 4-membered ring with one carbon substituent, and a second isomer based on a 3-membered ring with two carbons as substituents in total.
walkthrough:
Keep the atom count locked**
You need cyclic structures only, all with formula $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}$. Cyclopentane itself uses all 5 carbons in the ring. To make isomers, shrink the ring and put the leftover carbons outside as branches.

Build the first isomer**
Take a 4-membered cyclobutane ring. That uses 4 carbons, so one carbon is left. Attach it as a methyl group to give methylcyclobutane. In skeletal form this is a square with a short line for $\text{CH}_3$ on one corner.

Build a different second isomer**
Now take a 3-membered cyclopropane ring. That uses 3 carbons, so two carbons are left. You can attach them as one ethyl group to give ethylcyclopropane (triangle with a two-carbon chain), or as two methyl groups on the same carbon to give 1,1-dimethylcyclopropane. Either is correct as long as it is different from the first.

Final answer: Two different skeletal structures from: methylcyclobutane (4-membered ring with one $\text{CH}_3$ substituent); ethylcyclopropane (3-membered ring with one $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ substituent); 1,1-dimethylcyclopropane (3-membered ring with two $\text{CH}_3$ groups on the same carbon). Any two different structures.

hints: Recall the two ways a covalent bond can split in terms of electron sharing, one gives ions and the other gives radicals with single unpaired electrons.
walkthrough:
Picture the $\text{Cl-Cl}$ bond splitting**
In initiation, UV light provides energy to break $\text{Cl}_2$ into two $\text{Cl}^\bullet$ radicals. Each chlorine keeps one electron from the shared pair, so two neutral radicals form, not ions. Splitting the electron pair equally like this is homolytic fission.
Final answer: Homolytic fission.

hints: In propagation a radical reacts to make a new radical, so first think how $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}$ can lose one H to a chlorine radical while keeping the radical chain going.
For the second step think how the new carbon radical can react with a $\text{Cl}_2$ molecule to make the $\text{C-Cl}$ product and regenerate the chlorine radical.
walkthrough:
Follow the radical chain idea**
Propagation keeps radicals alive. One radical is used up and a fresh one is made, so the chain continues without UV light after initiation.

Write propagation 1 as H abstraction**
$\text{Cl}^\bullet$ attacks cyclopentane and removes a hydrogen atom: $$\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10} + \text{Cl}^\bullet \rightarrow \text{C}_5\text{H}_9^\bullet + \text{HCl}$$ The alkane becomes an alkyl radical and $\text{HCl}$ forms.

Write propagation 2 as Cl transfer**
The alkyl radical then attacks $\text{Cl}_2$: $$\text{C}_5\text{H}_9^\bullet + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_5\text{H}_9\text{Cl} + \text{Cl}^\bullet$$ The product $\text{C}_5\text{H}_9\text{Cl}$ forms and $\text{Cl}^\bullet$ is regenerated to start propagation 1 again.

Final answer: propagation 1: $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10} + \text{Cl}^\bullet \rightarrow \text{C}_5\text{H}_9^\bullet + \text{HCl}$
propagation 2: $\text{C}_5\text{H}_9^\bullet + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_5\text{H}_9\text{Cl} + \text{Cl}^\bullet$

hints: Think about what happens to the number of radicals when two radicals join together to make a stable molecule with all electrons paired.
walkthrough:
Spot radicals disappearing**
Here $\text{C}_5\text{H}_9^\bullet + \text{Cl}^\bullet \rightarrow \text{C}_5\text{H}_9\text{Cl}$ combines two radicals into one stable molecule. No new radical is produced, so the chain stops. Combining radicals to end the chain is termination.
Final answer: Termination.

hints: Look at reaction 3 in Fig. 3.2, cyclopentene with a $\text{C=C}$ bond becomes $\text{C}_5\text{H}_9\text{Cl}$, so think which hydrogen halide adds H and Cl across the double bond.
walkthrough:
Read the transformation**
Cyclopentene ($\text{C}_5\text{H}_8$) gains H and Cl to give chlorocyclopentane ($\text{C}_5\text{H}_9\text{Cl}$). This is electrophilic addition across the $\text{C=C}$ double bond. The suitable reagent is hydrogen chloride, $\text{HCl(g)}$.

hints: First find $\Delta H$ for reaction 1 (cyclopentene + $\text{H}_2$ to cyclopentane) using $\Delta H = \Sigma \Delta H_c(reactants) - \Sigma \Delta H_c(products)$.
Then use the Hess triangle in Fig. 3.2 to link reaction 1, reaction 2 and reaction 3, noting the direction of the arrows to get $\Delta H_2$.
walkthrough:
Calculate $\Delta H$ of hydrogenation from combustion data**
For any reaction, $\Delta H = \text{sum } \Delta H_c(reactants) - \text{sum } \Delta H_c(products)$ because combustion products are common. For reaction 1: $$\Delta H_1 = [\Delta H_c(\text{cyclopentene}) + \Delta H_c(\text{H}_2)] - [\Delta H_c(\text{cyclopentane})]$$ $$\Delta H_1 = [-3115 + (-286)] - [-3292] = -3401 + 3292 = -109 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$

Use the Hess triangle to find $\Delta H_2$**
Going from cyclopentene to $\text{C}_5\text{H}_9\text{Cl}$ directly is reaction 3 ($\Delta H_3 = -53$). The indirect route is reaction 1 backwards then reaction 2 forwards, but it is simpler to see that reaction 1 + $\Delta H_2$ must combine consistently around the cycle. With the arrows drawn, $\Delta H_3 = \Delta H_1 + \Delta H_2$ in effect for that loop, so: $$\Delta H_2 = \Delta H_3 - \Delta H_1 = -53 - (-109) = +56 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ The positive sign shows reaction 2 is endothermic.

Final answer: reaction 1: $\Delta H_1 = -3115 + (-286) - (-3292) = -109 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$
$\Delta H_2 = -53 - (-109) = +56 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

hints: Recall that hot concentrated acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$ cleaves the $\text{C=C}$ bond in a cyclic alkene and oxidises each alkene carbon fully to a carboxylic acid group.
walkthrough:
Open the ring at the double bond**
Cyclopentene is a 5-membered ring with one $\text{C=C}$. Hot concentrated $\text{MnO}_4^-/\text{H}^+$ breaks the double bond completely and adds oxygen to each end to give $-\text{COOH}$ groups. The ring therefore opens into a straight chain.

Count the chain**
Two carbons become the two $\text{COOH}$ carbons, the other three remain as $\text{CH}_2$ groups in the middle. That gives $\text{HOOC-CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{COOH}$, pentanedioic acid, formula $\text{C}_5\text{H}_8\text{O}_4$ which matches W.
Final answer: $\text{HOOCCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ (pentanedioic acid).

hints: Compare functional groups, cyclopentene has only C-H and C=C, while W has two carboxylic acid groups, so focus on bonds found only in $-\text{COOH}$ using Table 3.3.
Look for the very broad absorption around 2500 to 3000 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ and the strong sharp absorption around 1670 to 1740 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ in Fig. 3.3.
walkthrough:
List what is new in W**
Cyclopentene can show $\text{C-H}$ (2850-2950) and $\text{C=C}$ (1500-1680) only. W is a dicarboxylic acid, so it must show extra $\text{O-H}$ (carboxyl) and $\text{C=O}$ (carboxyl) absorptions that cyclopentene cannot show.

Assign the broad low wavenumber band**
The very broad trough centred near 3000 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ fits the 2500-3000 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ range for $\text{O-H}$ in a carboxyl group. Label this as 1 on Fig. 3.3 and write $\text{O-H}$ in Table 3.2.

Assign the strong carbonyl band**
The strong sharp dip near 1720 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ fits the 1670-1740 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ range for $\text{C=O}$ in a carboxyl group. Label this as 2 on Fig. 3.3 and write $\text{C=O}$ in Table 3.2.

Final answer: Absorption 1 at approx. 3000 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ (2500-3000 range): bond responsible $\text{O-H}$ in carboxyl.
Absorption 2 at approx. 1720 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ (1670-1740 range): bond responsible $\text{C=O}$ in carboxyl.
